summary: This Independent Submission describes using TLS 1.3 for machine-to-machine mutual authentication within federations. It is informational, not a standard, and it does not modify TLS.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers in a group can show each other ID cards using normal secure connections. No changes to the secure connection system are required.

questions: how does tls work in federations
subtitle: How organizations share secure connections with automatic identity verification.

tldr.problem: Organizations in a federation need machine-to-machine secure communication with automatic identity verification, without complex certificate management.
tldr.mechanism: MATF uses TLS 1.3 with public key pinning, where each organization's public keys are stored in a centrally managed, cryptographically signed federation metadata document.
tldr.outcome: Machines can authenticate each other without needing external certificate authorities, enabling pre-provisioning and secure service-to-service communication.

today: RFC 9932 is an Informational RFC documenting the MATF framework. It has not been obsoleted and is actively used in education sector federations to manage secure machine-to-machine communication.

sections.title: Introduction to MATF
sections.content:
The Mutually Authenticating TLS in Federations (MATF) framework enables machines within a federation to securely authenticate each other using TLS 1.3, without requiring changes to TLS itself or to common TLS libraries. A federation is a trusted network of organizations (called members) that share common security policies and use MATF for secure machine-to-machine communication.

MATF is designed for service-to-service and RESTful API communication, where machines need to prove their identity to other machines. It is not intended for browser-based authentication. The framework was developed to support education sector federations, where it has proven effective in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: MATF is a system that lets computers in an organization group prove who they are to each other using secure connections. Think of it like showing a trusted ID card instead of needing a separate person to verify you.

sections.title: How MATF Works
sections.content:
The MATF framework operates with three main roles. The federation operator is a trusted central authority that manages the federation, vets new members, and publishes a signed metadata document listing all members and their public keys. Each federation member is an approved organization that contributes its public key information to the federation metadata. Members use the federation metadata to discover other members and authenticate connections.

The framework relies on public key pinning, a technique where each member's public key (represented as a pin) is published in the federation metadata. When two machines connect over TLS 1.3, they exchange certificates containing their public keys. Both machines verify that the public key in the presented certificate matches a pin in the federation metadata. If there is no match, the connection is immediately terminated.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a trusted manager (the operator) who keeps a list of everyone in the group and their ID information. When one computer wants to talk to another, it checks the list to make sure the ID matches.

sections.title: Authentication and Trust
sections.content:
Trust in MATF starts with a single trust anchor: the public key used to verify the signature on the federation metadata itself. This key is published through a JSON Web Key Set (JWK Set), which may be distributed through multiple channels and verified using thumbprints to ensure authenticity. Federation members trust all information in the signed metadata because they trust the federation operator who signed it.

When a client machine initiates a connection to a server machine, it first obtains the server's public key pins from its local copy of the federation metadata. During the TLS handshake, both machines verify that each other's certificate public key matches a pin in the metadata. This process happens for both the client certificate (the client machine proving its identity to the server) and the server certificate (the server proving its identity to the client), enabling mutual authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone trusts one person's signature on the list. When computers connect, they both check the list to confirm the other person's ID is real.

sections.title: Federation Metadata
sections.content:
Federation metadata is published as a JSON Web Signature (JWS), a cryptographically signed JSON document. The metadata contains claims (statements) about each member entity, including required claims like issue time (iat), expiration time (exp), the federation's URI (iss), and the schema version. It also includes optional claims like a cache time-to-live (cache_ttl), which tells members how long they can cache the metadata locally.

The entities section lists all members, each with a unique entity_id, organization name, issuer certificates, and server or client endpoints. Each endpoint has pins (the public key fingerprints) that machines use for verification. Members can tag their endpoints (for example, "scim" or "api") to indicate what services they offer. The metadata is signed using JWS, with the algorithm (such as ES256) and a key identifier specified in the protected header.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is a signed document with entry details: when it was made, when it expires, everyone's ID information, and what services they offer.

sections.title: Managing Certificate Changes
sections.content:
Certificates expire or need to be replaced. MATF supports certificate rotation through a four-step process. First, the member submits updated metadata that includes the pin for the new certificate alongside the old pin, so both keys are trusted during the transition. The federation operator publishes the updated metadata, and all members refresh their local copies. The member then waits a propagation period to ensure all peers have the new pin cached. Finally, after members have had time to update, the old pin is removed from the metadata in a subsequent update, completing the rotation.

This approach avoids the complexity of certificate revocation systems, because trust is based directly on pinned public keys rather than on revocation status. When a key is no longer trusted, the pin is simply removed from the metadata.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone needs a new ID card, their name goes in the list with both the old and new cards for a while. Then later, the old card is removed.

sections.title: Real-World Deployments
sections.content:
MATF has been successfully deployed in the education sector. Skolfederation Moa is a Swedish federation enabling secure data exchange between educational platforms and schools, with active community participation. The Swedish National Agency for Education uses MATF within its national test platform to authenticate clients before secure data transfer. Sambruk's EGIL platform demonstrates MATF's adaptability to support digital services across municipalities.

These deployments have revealed important operational lessons. Maintaining accurate metadata ownership and contact information is essential for troubleshooting. Metadata expiration times must be reasonable to allow contingency planning during outages. Automated validation of submitted metadata becomes necessary as federations scale. Secure management of the federation's metadata signing private key with redundancy is critical to support both normal operations and fallback scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: Schools in Sweden use MATF to share information securely. Running a federation requires careful management of the master list and backup systems.
